blocks.content: COUNT versus COUNT star covered one specific, common instance of NULL behavior. NULL Handling steps back to cover the broader, genuinely important behavior behind that specific case, and several others that show up constantly across real SQL work, WHERE clauses, joins, aggregate functions, all of them.

This topic covers what NULL actually represents, why SQL uses three valued logic instead of simple true and false, the specific IS NULL syntax required to check for it correctly, and COALESCE, a genuinely practical function for substituting a real value wherever NULL shows up.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035775673-196847260.png
blocks.alt: NULL handling covers the broader behavior behind the specific NULL distinction already covered in the previous topic

blocks.content: 1. What NULL Actually Represents

NULL genuinely means unknown, or genuinely absent, it is not the same thing as zero, and it is not the same thing as an empty string, even though all three can feel similar at first glance. A number column containing NULL is not the same as that column containing the number zero.

A text column containing NULL is not the same as that column containing an empty string with no characters in it. NULL genuinely represents the complete absence of a known value, not a specific, known value that happens to be zero or blank.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035777883-672227729.png
blocks.alt: NULL genuinely means unknown or absent, not the same as zero for numbers, and not the same as an empty string for text

blocks.content: 2. Three Valued Logic

SQL genuinely uses three valued logic in comparisons, not just the simple true and false you might expect from other programming contexts. A comparison can evaluate to TRUE, to FALSE, or to UNKNOWN, specifically whenever NULL is genuinely involved in that comparison.

This UNKNOWN result is exactly why comparing a column against NULL using a standard equals sign never actually works the way you might intuitively expect, since the comparison genuinely evaluates to UNKNOWN, not to TRUE, even when comparing NULL against another NULL.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035779527-468672146.png
blocks.alt: SQL uses three valued logic: TRUE, FALSE, and UNKNOWN, with UNKNOWN genuinely resulting whenever NULL is involved in a comparison

3. A Worked Example

A concrete comparison shows this three valued logic applied directly. WHERE bonus equals NULL never actually matches anything at all, not even rows where bonus is genuinely NULL, since that comparison evaluates to UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN is treated the same as FALSE for the purpose of filtering rows.
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE bonus IS NULL;
blocks.code: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE bonus IS NULL;

codes.sql: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE bonus IS NULL;

blocks.content: WHERE bonus IS NULL genuinely matches rows where bonus is NULL, since IS NULL is a dedicated, specific check built exactly for this purpose, rather than relying on a standard equality comparison that was never designed to handle NULL correctly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035781044-811684856.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: bonus equals NULL never actually matches anything; bonus IS NULL genuinely matches rows where bonus is NULL

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Comparing a column against NULL using a standard equals sign, expecting it to work the way equality comparisons work for every other value. NULL genuinely requires the dedicated IS NULL or IS NOT NULL syntax specifically.
4. COALESCE, a Practical Way to Handle NULL
blocks.text: 4. COALESCE, a Practical Way to Handle NULL

blocks.content: COALESCE is a genuinely practical function that returns the first non NULL value from a list of arguments you provide, letting you substitute a real, meaningful default wherever a column would otherwise show NULL.
SELECT name, COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus FROM employees;
blocks.code: SELECT name, COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus FROM employees;

codes.sql: SELECT name, COALESCE(bonus, 0) AS bonus FROM employees;

blocks.content: This query genuinely returns the actual bonus value wherever one exists, but substitutes zero specifically for any employee whose bonus is NULL, letting downstream calculations, like summing this column, work correctly without needing to separately handle NULL values themselves.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035782609-72519859.png
blocks.alt: COALESCE returns the first non NULL value from a list, letting you substitute a real default wherever NULL would otherwise appear

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: COALESCE is genuinely useful specifically because SUM and AVG already exclude NULL automatically, but sometimes you actually want NULL treated as a specific value, like zero, for a particular calculation, and COALESCE is the real, practical tool for that substitution.
5. NULL in Comparisons, Generally

Any direct comparison involving NULL, equals, greater than, less than, genuinely evaluates to UNKNOWN, not to a real true or false, regardless of which specific comparison operator is actually being used.

IS NULL and IS NOT NULL specifically are the real exceptions, they are dedicated checks built exactly to handle NULL correctly, genuinely evaluating to a real, definite true or false, rather than the UNKNOWN result every other comparison produces when NULL is involved.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035784096-565852559.png
blocks.alt: Any direct comparison involving NULL genuinely evaluates to UNKNOWN; IS NULL and IS NOT NULL specifically evaluate to a real, definite true or false

blocks.content: 6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine correct NULL handling. Comparing against NULL with a standard equals sign instead of the dedicated IS NULL syntax, which genuinely never matches anything, silently returning fewer rows than actually intended. Assuming NULL behaves like zero for numbers or like an empty string for text, which genuinely produces wrong results in calculations and comparisons.
And forgetting that NOT applied to an UNKNOWN result is still genuinely UNKNOWN, not TRUE, a subtle detail that can silently affect filters built around NOT combined with a NULL involving comparison.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1784035785553-571349747.png
blocks.alt: Common mistakes: comparing against NULL with equals, assuming NULL behaves like zero or empty text, and forgetting NOT of UNKNOWN is still UNKNOWN
